rationale: Both critiques are sound and both propose a role-first decision record with slices, confidence intervals, explicit conflicts and revisit triggers. A contributes a shadow pilot, steelman arguments for each candidate and analysis of cases where models disagree, all of which are valuable. B's design is more rigorously built for the six-month defensibility requirement. It separates hard from soft constraints and derives meets/marginal/fails thresholds from the role context rather than from benchmark authors. It uses a Pareto view to eliminate dominated models, and it tags each metric with an evidence-quality label covering sample size and distribution match. It adds a sensitivity analysis showing how rankings flip under different weights or resampling. Its structured conflicting-evidence register records each resolution together with the assumption it depends on. The decision statement lists assumptions explicitly, and an appendix holds provenance and version hashes for reproducibility. Its critique also adds sharper points: composite weights are a disguised policy choice, and single rankings hide portfolio options. B's 'convex hull' wording is slightly loose for a Pareto frontier, but overall it is the more complete and auditable design.
